## Objectives

- Name the trade-off precisely: what you give up when accuracy goes up, and who pays
- Open a black box with three tools — importance, partial dependence, local explanations — and know what each one *cannot* tell you
- Decide, for a business or a clinical case, where on the accuracy–interpretability line to stand — and check which patients the model shortchanges
- Say it to a non-technical decision-maker without either lying or losing them

## Why a manager cares

::: {.subtitle-frame}
"The model said no. Why?" — and you must answer.
:::

| | The model decides | Who asks why |
|---|---|---|
| **Bank, retailer** | a declined loan · the 2 000 customers to call | the customer, the regulator, the sales director |
| **Health authority** | a readmission flag · who gets a case manager | the clinician who must act on it, the patient, the auditor |

: {tbl-colwidths="[20,42,38]"}

- **Regulation**: in the EU you owe an explanation for an automated decision that affects a person
- **Trust**: nobody acts on a score they cannot interrogate — a clinician least of all
- **Debugging**: the model that wins by 3 AUC points may have learned that `id > 5000` churns

Accuracy without interpretability is a liability you have not priced yet.

## [Section 1]{.section-kicker} The trade-off {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## The line, and where things sit on it

$$
\text{interpretable} \quad \longleftarrow\quad \text{linear} \;\;\; \text{tree} \;\;\; \text{GAM} \;\;\; \text{forest} \;\;\; \text{boosting} \;\;\; \text{network} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \text{flexible}
$$

- **Left**: the model *is* its explanation. A coefficient, a branch. You can defend it in a room.
- **Right**: the model is a function you can evaluate but not read. It is often more accurate, because reality is not linear.
- The middle is not empty: a GAM — additive, one smooth curve per variable — bends without hiding

::: {.callout-important title="The thesis of Module 2, from lecture 18"}
Flexibility and interpretability are traded, not combined. Every model on the right of the line owes you an explanation it cannot give by itself. The tools of this lecture are how you extract one — approximately, and with care.
:::

## Two kinds of question

- **Global**: *what does the model do, overall?* Which variables matter, and how does the prediction move with each?
- **Local**: *why this prediction, for this customer — or this patient?* What pushed her score above the threshold?

They need different tools. A good explanation to a board or a health authority is global; to a customer, a patient, or the clinician treating her, local.

## [Section 2]{.section-kicker} Global tools {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## Variable importance

For a forest: how much does the impurity fall, summed over every split that uses this variable? For any model: **permutation importance** — shuffle one column, remeasure test error, see how much it worsens.

- Ranks variables. Says *that* `tenure` matters, not *how*
- Correlated variables **share** importance — two near-copies each look half as important as the thing they measure
- Permutation importance is model-agnostic. Use it to compare a forest and a network on the same footing.

::: {.callout-note}
Importance is the first thing a manager asks for and the last thing you should stop at. A variable can be important because the model uses it *badly*.
:::

## Partial dependence

Fix one variable at a value $x$. Set it to $x$ for **every** row, predict, average. Repeat across $x$. Plot.

$$
\text{PD}_j(x) \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat f(x,\; x_{i,-j})
$$

- The *average* effect of variable $j$, with everything else as it is in the data
- Read it like a coefficient that is allowed to curve: churn rises steeply until 12 months of tenure, then flattens
- Its blind spot: **interactions**. If the effect of `monthly_charge` reverses between contract types, the average shows nothing. ICE plots — one curve per row, not averaged — reveal that.

## In R — global

```{.r code-line-numbers="1-2|4-5|7-8|10"}
library(iml); library(ranger)
rf <- ranger(churn ~ ., data = churn[tr, ], num.trees = 300, probability = TRUE)

pred <- Predictor$new(rf, data = churn[-tr, ], y = "churn", class = "yes")
imp  <- FeatureImp$new(pred, loss = "logLoss"); plot(imp)        # permutation importance

pdp  <- FeatureEffect$new(pred, feature = "tenure_months", method = "pdp+ice")
plot(pdp)                                                        # average curve + one per customer

FeatureEffect$new(pred, feature = c("monthly_charge", "contract"), method = "pdp") |> plot()
```

The last line: a two-way partial dependence. If the surface is not additive, the one-way plot was hiding something.

## [Drill 1]{.drill-kicker} What the diabetes score relies on

::: {.subtitle-frame}
In pairs · 10 minutes · 500 bagged trees on `MASS::Pima.tr`, scored on 332 test women · test AUC 0.828
:::

| Shuffled | `glu` | `age` | `bmi` | `ped` | `npreg` | `skin` | `bp` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| AUC points lost | 14.6 | 3.8 | 1.9 | 0.9 | 0.1 | −0.2 | −0.4 |

| Glucose at 2 h (mg/dl) | 80 | 100 | 120 | 140 | 160 | 180 | 200 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Partial dependence | 17% | 20% | 23% | 46% | 52% | 63% | 63% |

[`ped` family-history score · `skin` triceps skin fold · `bp` diastolic pressure · `npreg` pregnancies]{.muted}

1. Skin fold scores nothing, yet it correlates 0.66 with BMI. Is it irrelevant to diabetes?
2. Where does the glucose curve jump, and what does that tell the diabetologist?
3. The screening nurse has five minutes per woman. Which measurement leaves the form? One sentence.

## [Drill 1 · answer]{.drill-kicker} Read the model, then the medicine

- **Skin fold** is not irrelevant: it measures much of what BMI measures, and the trees took that information from BMI. Correlated variables share importance — here one took it all. Importance describes *this model, given the others*, not the disease
- **Glucose** doubles the risk between 120 and 140 mg/dl, from 23% to 46%: 140 at two hours is where guidelines start to call glucose tolerance impaired. The forest found the clinical threshold by itself — a model that agrees with what a diabetologist knows is one she will use
- **Skin fold and blood pressure** add nothing here (−0.2 and −0.4 are zero with noise). Refitted without them, the forest scores AUC 0.837 on the same test women

::: {.callout-tip title="A sentence that defends it"}
"Drop the skin fold: the score loses nothing without it, because BMI — ten seconds on a scale — already carries what the caliper measures."
:::

## [Section 3]{.section-kicker} Local tools {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## Explaining one prediction

**LIME**: perturb the inputs around *this* patient, fit a small **linear model** to the answers; its coefficients explain.

**Shapley values**: each variable's average contribution over all orderings. They **sum exactly** to this prediction minus the average one, which is why regulators like them.

| | LIME | Shapley (SHAP) |
|---|---|---|
| Idea | local linear surrogate | fair attribution |
| Guarantee | none — depends on the neighbourhood | additive, consistent |
| Cost | cheap | expensive; `TreeSHAP` fixes that for trees |
| Use it for | a quick "what drove this" | the answer you put in the letter |

## In R — local

```{.r code-line-numbers="1|3-4|6-7"}
one <- churn[-tr, ][17, ]                              # a customer the model flagged

sh <- Shapley$new(pred, x.interest = one)
plot(sh)                                               # contribution of each variable, this row

lime <- LocalModel$new(pred, x.interest = one, k = 5)  # 5-variable local linear model
plot(lime)
```

The Shapley plot reads: *average churn probability 27%; this customer 71%; month-to-month contract +18 points, three support calls +12, fibre +9, tenure of 40 months −6…* That is a sentence you can send.

## What none of this gives you

- **Causality.** *Tenure lowers churn* in the model does not mean *lengthening tenure would lower churn*. The model learned an association from customers who chose to stay.
- **Stability.** Explanations of the same prediction can differ between two equally accurate models. There is no unique "why".
- **Absolution.** An explained wrong decision is still a wrong decision.

::: {.callout-important title="Attention"}
The failure mode is *explanation theatre*: a SHAP plot next to a model nobody validated, to make an audience stop asking questions. The tools here are for finding out what the model does, not for making it look understood.
:::

## [Drill 2]{.drill-kicker} One patient, one explanation

::: {.subtitle-frame}
In pairs · 10 minutes · exact Shapley values, Drill 1's forest, test woman no. 101, aged 23
:::

Average risk in the training data **34.0%** · her risk **82.2%**

| | `glu` | `bmi` | `ped` | `skin` | `bp` | `npreg` | `age` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Her value | 179 | 44.1 | 0.686 | 27 | 90 | 0 | 23 |
| Points of risk | +35.0 | +8.2 | +7.9 | +1.4 | +0.9 | −0.1 | −5.1 |

1. Do the seven contributions account for her score?
2. Write two lines for her GP, and one sentence for her
3. She asks: *"If I bring my BMI down to 30, does my risk fall by those 8.2 points?"* Answer in one sentence

## [Drill 2 · answer]{.drill-kicker} An accounting identity, not a promise

- **Yes, exactly**: 34.0 + 35.0 + 8.2 + 7.9 + 1.4 + 0.9 − 0.1 − 5.1 = 82.2. Every point between the average woman and her goes to a variable; glucose alone is 35 of the 48.2
- **For the GP**: *82% against 34% on average; glucose 179 at two hours adds 35 points, BMI 44 and family history (above 4 women in 5) about 8 each; being 23 takes 5 off*
- **For her**: *your glucose test is the main reason: about 8 women in 10 with results like yours have diabetes, so the next step is a confirmation test*

::: {.callout-tip title="A sentence that defends it — the BMI question"}
"Those points describe how the model scored you, not what losing weight would do: that answer comes from clinical trials, and your doctor will give it to you with the confirmation test."
:::

[The model's own what-if — BMI 30, the rest unchanged — gives 70.5%: a fall of 11.7, not 8.2. And that too is an association, not an effect.]{.muted}

## [Section 4]{.section-kicker} Deciding {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## Where to stand, case by case

| Decision | Cost of a wrong prediction | Cost of no explanation | Stand |
|---|---|---|---|
| Who gets the catalogue | low | none | boosting, and move on |
| Whom to call for retention | medium | low | forest + importance |
| Credit limit | high | high, regulated | simple, or SHAP in every letter |
| Readmission flag on a chart | high | very high: a clinician acts | GAM or tree |

The deciding column is the third. And check the trade-off exists: on the diabetes data a logistic regression beats the forest, AUC 0.866 against 0.828.

## Who pays: accurate on average, unfair to a group

A model can be well calibrated overall and still fail one group of patients. Before it goes live, three checks:

- **By group**: calibration and who gets flagged, by area, sex, age band, country of birth. An average hides the group that pays
- **The label**: does the model predict what you care about, or a stand-in? *Cost* stands in for *need*, and worse for anyone who uses less care for the same illness
- **No explanation tool will show it**: importance and Shapley describe what the model does, and the model is doing exactly what it was asked

::: {.callout-note}
Not hypothetical: Obermeyer and colleagues (*Science*, 2019) found exactly this in a cost-based algorithm used by US health systems to pick patients for extra care.
:::

## Saying it to the board

- Lead with the **decision**, not the model: *we will contact these 2 000 customers first*
- One number for accuracy, with its baseline: *71% of churners caught, versus 27% by contacting at random*
- One picture: importance, or a partial dependence with a story — *risk is highest in the first year and after a support call*
- One sentence on the limit: *the model finds patterns, it does not know causes; the retention offer's effect we will measure with a test*

Everything else is for the appendix, and for you.

## [Drill 3]{.drill-kicker} Who gets the places

::: {.subtitle-frame}
In pairs · 10 minutes · a simulated district of 20 000 adults · 1 000 care-management places, to the highest predicted cost
:::

| | City | Inner areas |
|---|---|---|
| Share of residents | 74.8% | 25.2% |
| Chronic conditions per resident (mean) | 0.79 | 0.80 |
| Places in the programme | 893 | 107 |
| Chronic conditions, patients given a place (mean) | 3.52 | 4.44 |

1. The model predicts next year's cost within 1% in the city and 5% in the inner areas. Is it fair to inner-area patients?
2. Why is an inner-area patient given a place sicker than a city one?
3. What do you change before it goes live? The sentence for the director general.

## [Drill 3 · answer]{.drill-kicker} The label was the bias

- **Not fair**: a quarter of the residents, equally ill (0.80 conditions against 0.79), and 10.7% of the places — 107 of 1 000
- **To get a place, an inner-area patient needs about one condition more**: 4.44 against 3.52. The model is right about cost: services are far, so they cost less for the same illness. It was asked the wrong question
- **Change the label**: rank on predicted chronic conditions next year, not cost. The same 1 000 places then split 750 and 250 — three to one, like the residents

::: {.callout-tip title="A sentence that defends it"}
"We will rank patients on predicted illness, not predicted cost: on cost, inner-area patients needed one more chronic condition to get a place, because distance, not health, kept their bills low."
:::

## A model you cannot explain is a decision you cannot defend. Choose how much accuracy that is worth to you.  {.statement}
